LIMBA.CONTENTS:
OVERVIEW
I have a HO railroad set up that I put together 25-30 years ago. Its somewhat complex, sitting on a 12 foot by 4 foot table, and can run two trains independently on the mainline and have one or two more operating in a rail yard complete with sidings and a turntable. There are 13 rail switches (Y's) (with 11 controls since there are two pairs that are wired to operate together). There is a crossover and a reversing track on the main line. And there are 14 track blocks, sections of track that have independent power controls.
Needless to say, this is rather complex to operate, especially for one person. In addition to the 11 buttons to control the 13 switches, there are 14 power controls for the different blocks, 3 rheostats to control speed, 4 forward-off-reverse controls, and a control for the turntable. These are spread over two control panels.
One has to prevent trains from both derailing and crashing. Derailing occurs most commonly when a train tries to pass over a switch that is set incorrectly. It can also occur when a train is moving too fast around a curve or over a bridge. Collisions can occur when two trains converge on a switch or if two trains are on the same track and one is going faster than the other. The standard approach to preventing collisions is to ensure that only one train at a time is in a track block.
I want to control this setup from my computer. Moreover, I want to have a high level control so I can say things like "Take train A out of the yard, go around the outer loop 3 times, then around the inner loop twice, then reverse directions and go around the outer loop twice more before bringing the train back into the yard." At the same time, I want to ensure that the trains do not crash or derail. This is the system that should be written. Moreover it should be written as a generic system, able to control other layouts.
UNDERLYING HARDWARE
In order to have computer control of the HO layout, one needs to enable the computer to both understand the current conditions, for example, what state switches are in and where trains are, and to control things.
Our layout, because it is relatively old, used all manual controls. These include rheostats, buttons for each switch, and controls to select the power source and direction for each track block. Shortly after the layout was built, trains started to supportDigital Command Control (DCC). Here there is continuous power to all rails and the control is in the engine. DCC sends signals to the engines via pulses on top of the rail power. This is done using special controllers that are attached to the circuit. This allows each engine to independently go forwards or backwards and to controls speed. This type of control is much simpler and closer to the real world.
DCC, however, is starting to fall out of favor. Today one can find the equivalent controls using WiFi so that the engines can be controlled from ones phone or tablet and no special hardware is required. While DCC has been standardized, WiFi control has not.
While it is possible to create a circuit that would effectively actuate the original set of controls for the HO layout, we decided that it made more sense to upgrade the engines to use the latest technology. Again, while we could do this via DCC (there are Arduino-based DCC controllers), we decided that we wanted to go with WiFi and use the LocoFi implementation for the engines. Thus we have provided full power to all track segments and have the engines control their own speed and direction using embedded LocoFi controllers.
This means that the system needs to control the switches and signals, detect of the state of the trains, and control the speed and direction of the various engines. It does not need to control the power to the blocks. We inserted photo diodes in the tracks at key locations. These include on each side the gap between track blocks to detect when a train moves from one block to another; on entry to the two inputs to a switch to ensure the switch is set correctly before the train goes over it; and at locations where we might want a train to stop (red signal) before entering a new block. The sensors we use are not perfect and can given occasional false positive and false negative outputs. The program needs to accommodate this.
To detect train positions and control switches and signals we designed and built a set of track controllers. Each of these can control 3 switches, handle 8 sensors (photo-diodes), and set 6 signals. An additional controller can handle up to 40 sensors. These compliment the LocoFi engine controllers which control engine speed and direction. All controllers communicate over local WiFi using mDNS and short (4-64 byte) UDP messages. For the purpose of the software, one can assume the hardware is stable and not part of the program.
SOFTWARE OVERVIEW
The software we envision would allow both manual and automatic control of the complete layout. The user interface would display the current state of the switches, signals, and trains as the system knows them. It would let the user control the switches and signals directly. It would provide control of the engines using an interface similar to that offered by the LocoFi phone app, emulating the messages it sends to the engines.
The standard way of displaying a train layout, both in model railroading and for real trains, is to have an display an abstraction of the actual layout. This has a homomorphic mapping with the actual layout, which may omit some details such as curves. For a complex layout, there can be multiple such abstract displays that have connections from one to another. This can be seen in our initial system where the two control panels each have their own abstraction. The software we envision should provide such an abstraction as part of the interface and allow the user to control the various layout components from this abstraction. Note that since the system works in terms of this abstract layout, it cannot be dependent on absolute train positions.
The abstract layout is described in an XML file that provides positions for the tracks, switches, signals, sensors, and block boundaries. Tracks are indicated by connections between points (which may or may not relate to switches, signals or sensors). These are given in an arbitrary coordinate system and may not be exact. The software should load this file, make almost-straight lines straight, ensure that the track layout makes sense, associate points with blocks, and generally ensure the consistency of the input and the layout.
Both our hardware and the LocoFi hardware use mDNS over local WiFi to find the controlling application (or vice versa). Both use short UDP messages containing commands (to the hardware, e.g., engine speed, set switch, set signal) and status reports (e.g., sensor changed). The control software should find and connect to these devices, send them commands appropriately, and use them to monitor the state of the engines and layout. Moreover, the software should attempt to correct sensor errors whenever possible.
The software should to ensure the stability and safety of the system. It should prevent two trains from being in the same block at the same time. Because the system does not have absolute train position information, this is sufficient to prevent collisions. The system should ensure that a switch is set property before a train can pass over it. It should ensure that signals are set correctly and that trains obeyed the signals. It should enforce speed limits on specific sections of track (between two specified sensors).
The software should use the signals to ensure no two trains are in the same block. Each block has 3 states: EMPTY, INUSE, and RESERVED; where the RESERVED state is associated with a particular train. Signals can be RED or GREEN. Each signal is associated with an exit from a block and as sensor (point). The software should determine, based on the current switch settings, what block a train would go to from this signal (the target block). The signal should be set to GREEN only if the target block is EMPTY or if the target block is RESERVED for a train that is in the current block. Otherwise it should set it to RED. The software should stop a train at the sensor for a RED signal. To facilitate this, it should slow a train down in a block where an exit signal is RED. Note that RESERVED state and the target block need to be recomputed when the state of a block changes (e.g. when it goes to EMPTY) and when the state of switches change.
Switches can be either in state N (normal) or R (reverse). Generally N means that the switch is effectively a straight track while R means it is a curve.
The software should also provide the type of high level control that we envision where one could define a route for a train and have the train correctly follow that route while obeying the various safety conditions. It should identify loops from the layout as well as possible starting and ending points for a route.
The system should also be flexible and extensible. The embedded sensors do not provide complete information about train position. They have problems understanding the initial conditions, can miss trains at times, and there are significant spans of track with no sensors. The system should optionally allow a video camera aimed at the track to be used to obtain better information about the current state of trains. Note this isn't perfect either since there might be portions of the track, for example, tunnels, that would not be visible to the camera. The system should also be flexible in that it should be able to handle layouts beyond ours. We do not include examples of all types of tracks and conditions. For example, initially we only have 2-way switches while 3-way switches exist, and we have no X-crossings which induce other types of anti-collision constraints.
The system should be reactive and event driven. It should handle notifications from the various sensors and act based on them. It should not use polling.
The system is being designed for personal, local use. As such no access control is needed and data protection, backup, and system integrity are not particularly important.

## 1. SYSTEM OVERVIEW AND ARCHITECTURE
### 1.1 System Purpose The HO Railroad Control System provides computer-based control and management of model railroad layouts with safety enforcement, automated route following, and manual operation capabilities.
### 1.2 System Architecture - **Core Components**: Layout Abstraction Engine, Data Management System, Hardware Communication Layer, Safety Management System, Train Control Module, User Interface Layer - **Communication Protocol**: Local WiFi using mDNS discovery and UDP messaging (4-64 byte packets) - **Deployment Model**: Personal/local use, no network access or security requirements
## 2. LAYOUT ABSTRACTION AND DATA MANAGEMENT
### 2.1 Layout Description Format - **Input Format**: XML files describing layout components - **Required Elements**: - Track segments with coordinate points and connections - Switches (Y-shaped) with position definitions and control mappings - Signals with sensor associations and block exit mappings - Sensors (photo-diodes) at key locations - Track blocks with boundary definitions - Block power control information (not controlled by system) - **Coordinate System**: Arbitrary coordinate system, not necessarily exact
### 2.2 Layout Processing Requirements - **XML Parsing**: Load and parse layout description files - **Data Validation**: Validate track connectivity, switch configurations, block boundaries - **Layout Consistency**: - Make almost-straight lines straight - Ensure track layout makes logical sense - Associate points with blocks - Detect and report layout inconsistencies - **Block Management**: - Define 14 track blocks with independent power control - Map sensors to specific block boundaries - Validate block connectivity and topology
### 2.3 Data Persistence - **State Management**: Load and save system state information - **Configuration Storage**: Save layout configurations and user preferences - **Backup Mechanisms**: Periodic system state backup capability
## 3. HARDWARE COMMUNICATION AND CONTROL
### 3.1 Device Discovery and Connection - **Discovery Protocol**: mDNS over local WiFi network discovery - **Device Types**: - Track controllers (3 switches, 8 sensors, 6 signals per controller) - Sensor controllers (up to 40 sensors per controller) - LocoFi engine controllers - **Connection Management**: Establish and maintain connections with discovered devices
### 3.2 Communication Protocol - **Message Format**: UDP packets of 4-64 bytes - **Command Types**: - Switch control commands (set position) - Signal control commands (set state) - Engine speed/direction commands - Sensor reporting - **Status Reporting**: Device status updates and sensor change notifications
### 3.3 Hardware Control Operations - **Switch Control**: - Set switch positions based on route planning - Validate switch settings before allowing train passage - **Signal Control**: - Set signal states (RED/GREEN) based on safety logic - Associate signals with block exits and target blocks - **Engine Control**: - Emulate LocoFi phone app interface - Control engine speed and direction
## 4. SAFETY AND SITUATION MANAGEMENT
### 4.1 Block Management System - **Block States**: - EMPTY: No train in block - INUSE: Train currently in block - RESERVED: Block reserved for specific train - **State Transitions**: - Automatic state change based on sensor detection - Manual override capability - **Block Boundary Detection**: - Use photo-diode sensors at block boundaries - Handle false positive/negative sensor outputs
### 4.2 Signal Control Logic - **Signal State Determination**: - GREEN: Target block is EMPTY or RESERVED for current train - RED: Target block is INUSE by different train - **Signal Assignment**: - Associate each signal with specific block exit and sensor point - Compute target blocks based on current switch settings - **Train Stopping**: - Stop trains at sensors before RED signals - Slow trains in blocks with RED exit signals
### 4.3 Collision Prevention - **Block-Based Safety**: Prevent two trains in same block simultaneously - **Switch Verification**: Ensure switches are set correctly before train passage - **Signal Enforcement**: Enforce signal compliance for train movement - **Speed Limit Management**: Apply speed limits on specific track sections
## 5. TRAIN CONTROL AND ROUTE PLANNING
### 5.1 Manual Train Control - **Engine Interface**: - Speed control (0-100%) - Direction control (forward/reverse) - Emergency stop functionality - **Control Emulation**: - Replicate LocoFi phone app messaging interface - Support all standard engine control commands
### 5.2 Automated Route Following - **Route Definition**: - Define routes for trains using abstract layout coordinates - Specify starting and ending points - **Loop Detection**: Identify loops in the layout topology - **Route Planning**: - Compute optimal paths between specified points - Handle multiple possible routes - **Safety Integration**: - Ensure route following maintains safety constraints - Adjust routes dynamically based on current conditions
### 5.3 Route Execution - **Step-by-Step Movement**: Execute routes one segment at a time - **Switch Management**: Automatically set switches required for route - **Signal Coordination**: Coordinate with signal system during route execution - **Dynamic Adaptation**: Modify route execution in response to changing conditions
## 6. SENSOR MANAGEMENT AND ERROR CORRECTION
### 6.1 Sensor Data Processing - **Sensor Integration**: - Handle 8 sensors per track controller - Handle up to 40 sensors per sensor controller - **Data Quality Management**: - Detect and correct false positive/negative readings - Implement sensor redundancy strategies - **Position Estimation**: - Estimate train positions in unsensed sections - Use historical data for position prediction
### 6.2 Error Correction Capabilities - **Sensor Validation**: - Cross-reference multiple sensors for verification - Implement consistency checking algorithms - **False Reading Handling**: - Filter out spurious sensor readings - Apply temporal smoothing techniques - **Recovery Mechanisms**: - Reinitialize sensor states when errors detected - Maintain system reliability despite sensor imperfections
## 7. USER INTERFACE REQUIREMENTS
### 7.1 Display Abstraction - **Visual Layout**: - Abstract representation of physical layout - Homomorphic mapping to actual track configuration - Support for multiple display views - **Component Visualization**: - Switch positions (current state) - Signal states (RED/GREEN) - Train positions and movement indicators - Block status indicators
### 7.2 Control Interface - **Manual Controls**: - Direct switch position control - Signal state setting - Engine speed/direction control - **Route Planning Tools**: - Route definition interface - Start/stop route execution - Route modification capabilities - **Status Monitoring**: - Real-time system status display - Error and warning notifications - Historical data access
## 8. EXTENSIBILITY AND FLEXIBILITY
### 8.1 Layout Flexibility - **Component Support**: - Handle different switch types (2-way, 3-way) - Support various track configurations - Accommodate X-crossings and other complex geometries - **Configuration Management**: - Support for multiple layout configurations - Easy configuration switching
### 8.2 Video Integration - **Camera Interface**: - Integrate video feeds from track cameras - Provide enhanced train position detection - **Visibility Limitations**: - Handle tunnel and obscured sections - Combine camera data with sensor information - **Fallback Mechanisms**: - Operate without camera integration - Use sensor data as primary source
## 9. SYSTEM OPERATIONS AND EVENTS
### 9.1 Event-Driven Architecture - **Real-time Processing**: - React to sensor changes immediately - Process device status updates asynchronously - **Notification System**: - Push notifications for system events - Alert mechanisms for safety violations - **Event Queue Management**: - Prioritize critical safety events - Handle concurrent event processing
### 9.2 System Responsiveness - **Latency Requirements**: - Real-time response to sensor changes - Immediate command execution - **Resource Management**: - Efficient memory usage - Optimize processing for real-time constraints
## 10. PERFORMANCE AND RELIABILITY REQUIREMENTS
### 10.1 System Reliability - **Stable Operation**: - Continuous operation without system crashes - Graceful handling of hardware failures - **Fault Tolerance**: - Continue operation with degraded sensor performance - Maintain safety enforcement despite individual component failures
### 10.2 Performance Characteristics - **Response Time**: - Sensor event processing within 50ms - Command execution within 100ms - **Throughput**: - Handle multiple concurrent trains - Process sensor updates at required frequency - **Scalability**: - Support for expanded layout configurations - Efficient handling of increased component counts
## 11. SYSTEM INTEGRATION REQUIREMENTS
### 11.1 Hardware Integration - **Controller Compatibility**: - Support all track controllers (3 switches, 8 sensors, 6 signals) - Support sensor controllers (40 sensors) - Integrate with LocoFi engine controllers - **Network Integration**: - Local WiFi network communication - mDNS discovery compatibility
### 11.2 Software Integration - **External Dependencies**: - Minimal external libraries required - Standard networking and XML processing libraries - **API Compatibility**: - Support for LocoFi protocol emulation - Extensible architecture for future enhancements
## 12. TESTING AND VALIDATION
### 12.1 Safety Validation - **Collision Prevention Testing**: - Verify block-based safety enforcement - Test switch verification logic - Validate signal control algorithms - **Sensor Error Handling**: - Test false positive/negative handling - Validate error recovery mechanisms
### 12.2 Functional Testing - **Route Following Validation**: - Test automated route execution - Verify safety constraint enforcement - **Interface Testing**: - Validate user control capabilities - Test display accuracy and responsiveness
This comprehensive requirement specification ensures the HO Railroad Control System meets all functional, safety, and operational needs while maintaining flexibility for future enhancements.
